title: Look Beyond Uptime to Measure Healthcare IT Reliability
summary: See why healthcare IT reliability starts with the service clinicians use and extends across the technologies, dependencies and teams that support it.
body_markdown:
Healthcare IT teams spend a lot of time measuring reliability, and for good reason. Uptime, latency, capacity and platform health help show whether the infrastructure beneath an application is available and performing as expected. Those signals, however, describe only part of the service a clinician actually uses.


Clinical applications almost always rely on multiple parts of the IT environment working together. That can include virtualization, storage, networking, databases, operating systems, load balancers, identity services, backups and application services. A problem anywhere in that chain can affect the service even when most of the underlying infrastructure appears healthy.


In my experience, the most useful way to think about reliability is to start with the service the clinician needs, then work backward through the technologies and teams that deliver it. Starting with the service gives teams a clearer basis for how they monitor the environment, respond to incidents and improve reliability over time.


### Start with the service, then work backward


Infrastructure teams watch CPU, memory and latency, along with storage capacity, backup status, network health and platform availability. Together, those signals help teams assess component health, capacity and performance. They can also point to conditions that may degrade a service, but they cannot tell you on their own whether the complete service is available to the clinician.


To assess service reliability, teams need to connect those infrastructure signals to the application and the experience of the people using it. That requires visibility across the technologies and services that support the application, not just the health of each component in isolation.


I would start by asking whether the clinician can sign in and use the application, whether the application can reach its database and other dependent services and whether performance is within the expected range. Once teams understand how the service is affected, they can work backward through the service chain and use infrastructure metrics to narrow the cause.


### Organize incident response around service impact


Operational responsibility for the technologies behind a healthcare application is usually divided by technical domain. One team manages virtualization, another storage, another networking and another the application itself. That structure gives each team clear ownership, while the service clinicians use crosses those boundaries.


During an incident, individual teams may see healthy signals within their own domain while the application remains unavailable or degraded. If the response stays focused on individual components, teams can lose time moving between technical domains before they isolate the source of the problem.


Starting with the impact on the service gives every team a common point of reference. Teams still investigate their own domains, but they do it against a shared picture of the application, its dependencies and the path the user takes to reach it. Clear ownership and escalation paths help teams move across technical boundaries, isolate the source of the problem and restore the service more efficiently.


### Give teams visibility across the service chain


To troubleshoot a service end to end, teams need visibility across the technologies and services that support it. A single application service can span VMware-based virtual machines, databases, container platforms such as Kubernetes, identity services, storage, networking, security controls and external services, each with its own telemetry, operating model and support team.


As private cloud environments incorporate more automation, container platforms and security controls, the number of dependencies behind a single application can grow as well. Teams also need to understand how those technologies connect, where ownership changes and what relationships come into play when service performance degrades or availability is disrupted. Architecture documentation and dependency maps help, and engineers also need practical experience troubleshooting across those boundaries.


During a service disruption, the first visible symptom may appear far from the underlying cause. Users may experience the problem in the application while the source sits in identity, networking, storage, a database or another dependent service. Connecting those signals quickly helps teams focus on the right part of the service chain.


### Use AI to improve signal without losing context


AI can support cross-domain troubleshooting by analyzing telemetry, correlating events and surfacing patterns that help engineers narrow the source of a service problem. AI is most useful when engineers can interpret those signals in the context of the specific environment. They need to understand the relationships among its components and the operational consequences of a proposed action before they act on a recommendation.


I will explore that relationship in more detail in a separate post on Epic, cloud and AI integration. Here, the reliability point is straightforward: AI-generated insights are most useful when teams already understand how the service and its underlying technologies work together.


### Measure reliability from the service backward


Healthcare IT reliability starts with whether the complete service is available and performing as expected. Infrastructure metrics still tell teams important information about component health, capacity and performance, but those signals are most useful when they are connected to the application or workflow they support.


The technology underneath that service will continue to change. But the operating question stays the same: Can clinicians and other users access the service they need when they need it? Starting there gives infrastructure and operations teams a clearer basis for monitoring service health, responding to incidents and improving reliability across the environment.
